title: Part 6, Chapter 6
paragraphs: He spent that evening until ten o'clock going from one low haunt to another. Katia turned up again and sang another gutter song about a certain "villain and tyrant" who
"began kissing Katia."

Svidrigailov treated Katia, the organ-grinder, some singers, the waiters, and two little clerks. He was particularly drawn to these clerks by the fact that both had crooked noses — one bent to the left, the other to the right. They eventually took him to a pleasure garden, where he paid their entrance. The garden contained one scraggly three-year-old pine tree and three bushes, plus a "Vauxhall" that was really a drinking establishment where tea was also served, with a few green tables and chairs set around it. A chorus of wretched singers and a drunken but deeply depressed German clown from Munich with a red nose entertained the patrons. The clerks got into a quarrel with some other clerks, and a fight seemed imminent. Svidrigailov was asked to arbitrate. He listened for a quarter of an hour, but they were shouting so loudly that it was impossible to understand them. The only clear fact was that one of them had stolen something and had even managed to sell it on the spot to a Jew, but refused to split the proceeds with his companion. It turned out the stolen item was a teaspoon belonging to the Vauxhall. Once this was discovered, the situation threatened to become serious. Svidrigailov paid for the spoon, got up, and walked out. It was about six o'clock. He hadn't touched a drop of wine the entire time, ordering tea mostly for appearances.

It was a dark, stifling evening. Around ten, threatening storm clouds gathered. There was a clap of thunder and the rain came down like a waterfall — not in drops but in sheets beating against the earth. Lightning flashed every minute, and each flash lasted long enough to count to five.

Soaked to the skin, he went home, locked himself in, opened the bureau, and took out all his money. He tore up two or three papers. Then, putting the money in his pocket, he was about to change his clothes, but looked out the window, listened to the thunder and the rain, and gave up the idea. He took his hat and went out without locking the door. He went straight to Sonia. She was home.

She wasn't alone: the four Kapernaumov children were with her, and she was giving them tea. She received Svidrigailov in respectful silence, looking with wonder at his soaking clothes. The children fled at once in indescribable terror.
Svidrigailov sat down at the table and asked Sonia to sit beside him. She timidly prepared to listen.

"I may be going to America, Sofya Semyonovna," said Svidrigailov, "and since I'm probably seeing you for the last time, I've come to make some arrangements. Well, did you see the lady today? I know what she told you — you don't need to repeat it." Sonia made a movement and blushed. "Those people have their own way of doing things. As for your sisters and your brother, they're truly provided for, and the money assigned to them has been deposited safely — I have the receipts. You'd better keep them yourself, in case anything happens. Here — take them. Well, that's settled. And here are three five-percent bonds worth three thousand rubles. Take these for yourself — entirely for yourself, and let this remain strictly between us. No one else should know, whatever you may hear. You'll need the money, because going on living the old way, Sofya Semyonovna, is wrong — and besides, there's no need for it now."
"I'm so grateful to you, and so are the children and my stepmother," Sonia said hurriedly, "and if I've said so little... please don't think me ungrateful..."
"Enough, enough!"
"As for the money, Arkady Ivanovitch, I'm very grateful, but I don't need it now. I can always earn my own living. Don't think me ungrateful. If you're so charitable, that money..."

"It's for you, Sofya Semyonovna — for you. And please don't waste time arguing. I haven't got time for it. You'll need it. Rodion Romanovitch has two choices: a bullet in the brain, or Siberia." Sonia stared at him wildly and flinched. "Don't be alarmed — I know everything from him personally, and I'm no gossip. I won't tell anyone. You gave him good advice when you told him to turn himself in and confess. It would be far better for him. Well, if it turns out to be Siberia, he'll go — and you'll follow him. That's how it is, isn't it? And if so, you'll need money. You'll need it for him — do you understand? Giving it to you is the same as giving it to him. Besides, you promised Amalia Ivanovna you'd pay what's owed. I heard you. How can you take on such obligations so carelessly, Sofya Semyonovna? It was Katerina Ivanovna's debt, not yours — you should have ignored the German woman. You can't get through the world that way. If anyone ever asks about me — tomorrow or the day after, you'll be asked — don't say anything about my coming here tonight, and don't show the money to anyone or breathe a word about it. Well, goodbye." He rose. "My regards to Rodion Romanovitch. By the way — you'd be wise to keep the money with Mr. Razumikhin for now. You know Mr. Razumikhin? Of course you do. He's a decent fellow. Take it to him tomorrow or... when the time comes. Until then, hide it carefully."
Sonia sprang up from her chair and stared at Svidrigailov in dismay. She desperately wanted to speak, to ask something, but for the first moments she didn't dare and didn't know how to begin.
"How can you... how can you be going out now, in this rain?"

"Well, if I'm heading off to America, should I let a little rain stop me? Ha, ha! Goodbye, Sofya Semyonovna, my dear! Live — and live long. You'll be of use to others. By the way... tell Mr. Razumikhin I send my greetings. Tell him: Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigailov sends his greetings. Be sure you do."
He left, leaving Sonia in a state of bewildered anxiety and vague dread.

It emerged later that the same evening, just after eleven-twenty, he made another very eccentric and unexpected visit. The rain was still coming down. Drenched to the skin, he appeared at the tiny apartment where his fiancée's parents lived, on Third Street in Vasilievsky Island. He had to knock for some time before he was let in, and his visit initially caused great consternation. But Svidrigailov could be very charming when he chose, and the parents' first, quite sensible assumption — that Svidrigailov had drunk so much he didn't know what he was doing — vanished almost immediately. The decrepit father was wheeled in by the tender, sensible mother, who as usual launched the conversation with various roundabout questions. She never asked anything directly: she would begin by smiling and rubbing her hands, then, when she absolutely had to find something out — such as when Svidrigailov would like the wedding — she'd start with eager questions about Paris and court life, only gradually working her way to Third Street. On other occasions this had been quite impressive, but tonight Arkady Ivanovitch seemed unusually impatient and insisted on seeing his fiancée immediately, despite being told she had already gone to bed. The girl appeared, of course.

Svidrigailov informed her at once that urgent business required him to leave Petersburg for a time, and therefore he was bringing her fifteen thousand rubles as a gift, which he'd long intended to give her before the wedding. The logical connection between this gift, his imminent departure, and the absolute necessity of visiting in a downpour at midnight was never made clear. But everything went remarkably smoothly; even the inevitable exclamations of wonder and questions were unusually few and restrained. On the other hand, the gratitude expressed was most effusive, reinforced by tears from the most sensible of mothers. Svidrigailov got up, laughed, kissed his fiancée, patted her cheek, declared he'd return soon, and noticing in her eyes — alongside childish curiosity — a kind of earnest, silent question, he paused and kissed her again, though he felt genuine irritation at the thought that his gift would be immediately locked away by the most sensible of mothers. He left them all in a state of extraordinary excitement, but the tender mama, speaking quietly in a half-whisper, resolved most of their doubts by concluding that Svidrigailov was a great man, a man of great affairs and connections and great wealth — one couldn't tell what he had in his head. He might start a journey and hand out money just as the fancy took him, so there was nothing surprising in it. It was odd that he was so wet, of course, but the English, for instance, were even more eccentric, and people of the upper classes didn't care what others said and didn't stand on ceremony. Perhaps he'd come like that on purpose, to show he wasn't afraid of anyone. Above all, not a word to anyone about it — God knew what might come of it — and the money must be locked up. It was most fortunate that Fedosya the cook hadn't left the kitchen. And above all, not a word to that old cat Madame Resslich. They sat whispering until two in the morning, but the girl went to bed much earlier, amazed and rather sorrowful.

Svidrigailov, meanwhile, at exactly midnight, was crossing the bridge back to the mainland. The rain had stopped and a roaring wind had risen. He began to shiver, and for one moment he stared at the black waters of the Little Neva with a look of special interest, almost inquiry. But he soon decided it was too cold standing by the water; he turned and headed toward Y— Prospect. He walked along that endless street for a long time, nearly half an hour, stumbling more than once in the dark on the wooden pavement, but constantly scanning the right side of the street for something. He'd noticed recently, passing through this area, a wooden hotel of a fair size, and its name — something like the Adrianople — had stuck in his memory. He was right: the hotel was conspicuous enough in that godforsaken place to be visible even in the dark. It was a long, blackened wooden building, and despite the late hour, lights glowed in the windows and there were signs of life inside. He went in and asked a ragged fellow in the corridor for a room. The man looked Svidrigailov up and down, pulled himself together, and led him at once to a cramped, tiny room at the far end of the corridor, under the stairs. There was nothing else — everything was taken. The ragged man looked at him expectantly.
"Is there tea?" Svidrigailov asked.
"Yes, sir."
"What else?"
"Veal, vodka, appetizers."
"Bring me tea and veal."
"You don't want anything else?" the man asked with apparent surprise.
"Nothing."
The ragged man withdrew, completely disillusioned.

"Must be a decent place," Svidrigailov thought. "How is it I didn't know about it? I must look like someone coming from a café chantant who's had some adventure along the way. I wonder who else stays here?"

He lit the candle and examined the room more carefully. It was so low-ceilinged that Svidrigailov could barely stand upright. It had one window; the bed was extremely dirty, and the plain-stained chair and table nearly filled the space. The walls seemed to be made of planks, covered with shabby wallpaper so torn and dusty that the pattern was unrecognizable, though the general color — yellow — could still be made out. One wall was cut short by the sloping ceiling: the room wasn't an attic, but lay directly beneath the stairs.

Svidrigailov set down the candle, sat on the bed, and sank into thought. But a strange, persistent murmur from the next room — sometimes rising to a shout — caught his attention. The murmuring had been going on since he entered. He listened: someone was scolding and almost tearfully berating another person, but only one voice could be heard.

Svidrigailov got up, shaded the candle with his hand, and noticed light seeping through a crack in the wall. He went over and peered through. The neighboring room, somewhat larger than his, had two occupants. One, a very curly-haired man with a red, inflamed face, stood in an orator's pose — coatless, legs spread wide for balance — thumping his own chest. He was reproaching the other man for being a beggar, for having no standing whatsoever, declaring he'd pulled him out of the gutter and could throw him back whenever he pleased, and that only Providence could see the truth of it. The object of this tirade sat in a chair looking like a man who desperately needs to sneeze but can't. He would occasionally turn sheepish, bleary eyes on the speaker but obviously had no idea what was being said and barely heard it. A candle was guttering on the table amid glasses, a nearly empty bottle of vodka, bread and cucumbers, and glasses with dregs of stale tea. After studying this scene, Svidrigailov turned away indifferently and sat back on the bed.

The ragged attendant returned with the tea and couldn't resist asking once more whether the gentleman wanted anything else. Receiving another negative, he withdrew for good. Svidrigailov drank a glass of tea to warm himself but couldn't eat a bite. He was beginning to feel feverish. He took off his coat, wrapped himself in the blanket, and lay down. He was annoyed. "It would have been better to be healthy for the occasion," he thought with a grim smile. The room was stuffy, the candle burned dimly, the wind howled outside, a mouse scratched in the corner, and the whole room smelled of mice and leather. He lay in a kind of half-dream: one thought chased another. He longed to fix his imagination on something. "There must be a garden under the window," he thought. "The sound of trees. How I hate the sound of trees on a stormy night in the dark! They give you a horrible feeling." He remembered disliking it when he'd passed Petrovsky Park earlier. This reminded him of the bridge over the Little Neva, and he felt cold again as he had standing there. "I've never liked water," he thought, "not even in a painting." He suddenly smiled at a strange idea: "You'd think at a time like this, all these questions of taste and comfort shouldn't matter — and yet I've become more particular, like an animal that picks a special spot for... such an occasion. I should have gone to Petrovsky Park! I suppose it seemed too dark, too cold — ha-ha! As if I needed pleasant sensations!... By the way, why haven't I blown out the candle?" He blew it out. "They've gone to bed next door," he thought, seeing no light through the crack. "Well then, Marfa Petrovna — now would be the time for you to appear. It's dark, and the place couldn't be more fitting. But of course, now you won't come!"

He suddenly recalled how, an hour before carrying out his plan with Dunya, he had recommended Raskolnikov to entrust her to Razumikhin's care. "I suppose I really did say it, as Raskolnikov guessed, just to tease myself. But what a rogue that Raskolnikov is! He's been through a lot. He may become a successful rogue in time, once he's gotten over his foolishness. But right now he's too hungry for life. These young men are contemptible on that score. Well, to hell with him! Let him do as he likes. It's nothing to do with me."

He couldn't sleep. Gradually Dunya's image rose before him, and a shudder passed over him. "No, I have to put that aside now," he thought, rousing himself. "I need to think about something else. It's strange and funny: I've never felt great hatred for anyone, never particularly wanted revenge — that's a bad sign, a bad sign. I never liked quarreling and never lost my temper — another bad sign. And those promises I made to her — damn it! But who knows — maybe she could have made a new man of me somehow..."

He ground his teeth and fell silent again. Dunya's image rose once more — exactly as she'd looked after firing the first shot, when she'd lowered the revolver in terror and stared blankly at him, so that he could have seized her twice over without her lifting a hand to defend herself — if only he hadn't reminded her. He remembered how in that instant he had almost felt sorry for her, how something had clutched at his heart...
"Damn! These thoughts again! I have to stop this!"

He was dozing off; the feverish chill had ceased. Suddenly something seemed to scurry over his arm and leg beneath the blanket. He started. "Ugh, damn — must be a mouse," he thought. "It's the veal I left on the table." He hated the idea of throwing off the blanket, getting up, getting cold — but suddenly something unpleasant ran over his leg again. He flung off the blanket and lit the candle. Shaking with feverish chills, he bent down to examine the bed: nothing. He shook the blanket and suddenly a mouse darted out onto the sheet. He tried to catch it, but the mouse zigzagged back and forth without leaving the bed, slipped through his fingers, ran across his hand, and suddenly shot under the pillow. He threw down the pillow, but instantly felt something leap onto his chest and dash across his body and down his back under his shirt. He flinched violently and woke up.
The room was dark. He was lying on the bed, wrapped in the blanket as before. Wind was howling at the window. "How disgusting," he thought with irritation.

He sat up on the edge of the bed with his back to the window. "Better not to sleep at all," he decided. A cold, damp draft seeped from the window. Without getting up, he pulled the blanket over himself and wrapped it tight. He wasn't thinking about anything and didn't want to think. But images rose one after another, incoherent scraps of thought without beginning or end drifted through his mind. He began sinking into drowsiness. Perhaps the cold, or the damp, or the darkness, or the wind howling outside and shaking the trees stirred a persistent craving for the fantastical. He kept dwelling on flowers. He imagined a lovely flower garden, a bright, warm, almost hot day — a holiday, Trinity Sunday. A fine, lavish country house in the English style, overgrown with fragrant flowers, with flower beds running all around it. The porch, twined with climbing plants, was surrounded by beds of roses. A light, cool staircase carpeted with rich rugs was adorned with rare plants in porcelain pots. He noticed especially, in the windows, bouquets of tender white narcissus, heavily fragrant, drooping over their bright green, thick long stems. He was reluctant to move away from them, but he went up the stairs and entered a large, tall drawing room — and again, everywhere, at the windows, by the doors onto the balcony, on the balcony itself — flowers. The floors were strewn with freshly cut, fragrant hay; the windows were open; a fresh, cool, light breeze drifted into the room. Birds chirped outside the window. In the middle of the room, on a table draped in a white satin shroud, stood a coffin. The coffin was covered in white silk with a thick white frill; wreaths of flowers surrounded it on all sides. Among the flowers lay a girl in a white muslin dress, arms crossed and pressed to her breast, as if carved from marble. But her loose fair hair was wet; a wreath of roses circled her head. Her stern, already rigid profile seemed chiseled from marble too, and the smile on her pale lips held an immense, unchildlike sorrow and sorrowful appeal. Svidrigailov knew that girl. No holy icon stood beside the coffin, no candle burned, no prayers were said. The girl had drowned herself. She was only fourteen, but her heart was broken. She had destroyed herself, crushed by an insult that had appalled and stunned her childish soul, had smeared her angel purity with undeserved shame, and torn from her a last cry of despair — unheard, brutally ignored — on a dark night, in the cold and wet, while the wind howled...

Svidrigailov came to himself, rose from the bed, and went to the window. He found the latch and opened it. The wind lashed into the tiny room, stinging his face and chest through his shirt with an icy bite. Under the window there must have been something like a garden — a pleasure garden, apparently. There, too, tea-tables probably stood and songs were sung during the day. Now rain flew in from the trees and bushes; it was as dark as a cellar, and he could barely make out a few dim shapes. Svidrigailov leaned on the windowsill with both elbows and stared into the darkness for five minutes. The boom of a cannon, then another, sounded through the dark night. "The flood signal! The river is rising," he thought. "By morning, the water will be swirling through the streets in the low-lying parts, flooding the basements and cellars. The cellar rats will swim out, and people will curse in the wind and rain as they drag their belongings upstairs. What time is it?" And just as he thought it, a clock somewhere nearby, ticking hurriedly, struck three.

"In another hour it'll be light. Why wait? I'll go now — straight to the park. I'll pick a big bush, one drenched with rain, so that when you brush against it with your shoulder, millions of drops shower down on your head."

He stepped away from the window, closed it, lit the candle, put on his vest, overcoat, and hat, and went out with the candle into the corridor to find the ragged attendant, who would be sleeping somewhere amid candle-stubs and assorted rubbish, to pay for the room and leave. "This is the best moment. I couldn't choose a better one."

He walked for some time through a long, narrow corridor without finding anyone and was about to call out when suddenly, in a dark corner between an old cupboard and the doorframe, he noticed a strange object that seemed to be alive. He bent down with the candle and saw a little girl — no more than five years old — shivering and crying, her clothes as wet as a sopping dishrag. She didn't seem afraid of Svidrigailov but stared at him with blank amazement from her big dark eyes. Now and then she sobbed, the way children do when they've been crying a long time but are beginning to calm down. The child's face was pale and exhausted; she was numb with cold. "How could she have gotten here? She must have hidden and never slept." He began questioning her. The child suddenly came to life, chattering in her baby language about "mommy" and how "mommy would hit her" and about some cup she'd "bwoken." She prattled on without stopping. He could only piece together from her words that she was a neglected child whose mother — probably a drunken cook employed at the hotel — beat and terrorized her. The girl had broken one of her mother's cups and was so frightened that she'd run away the evening before, hidden outside in the rain for ages, finally crept inside, hidden behind the cupboard, and spent the whole night there, crying and shivering in the damp, the dark, and the terror of being beaten. He picked her up, carried her to his room, set her on the bed, and began undressing her. Her torn shoes, on stockingless feet, were as wet as if they'd been standing in a puddle all night. When he'd undressed her, he put her in the bed, covered her up, and wrapped her in the blanket from head to toe. She fell asleep instantly. Then he sank back into gloomy brooding.

"What a fool I am, getting involved," he thought with a sudden feeling of oppressive annoyance. "What idiocy!" In his vexation he picked up the candle, intending to find the ragged attendant and leave at once. "Damn the child!" he thought, reaching for the door — but he turned back to check whether she was sleeping. He carefully lifted the blanket. The child was sleeping soundly and had gotten warm. Her pale cheeks had flushed. But the flush seemed brighter and coarser than a normal rosy glow of childhood. "It's a fever flush," Svidrigailov thought. It looked more like the flush from alcohol — as though she'd been given a full glass of wine. Her crimson lips were hot and burning. But what was this? He suddenly thought her long dark lashes were quivering, as though the lids were lifting and a sly, crafty eye was peeping out with an unchildlike wink — as if the little girl weren't asleep at all but pretending. Yes — that was it. Her lips parted in a smile. The corners of her mouth quivered, as though she were trying to hold it back. But now she gave up all pretense. It was a grin — a broad grin. There was something shameless, provocative in that utterly unchildlike face; it was corruption, the face of a prostitute, the brazen face of a French harlot. Now both eyes were open wide, turning a glowing, shameless stare on him; they laughed, they invited... There was something infinitely hideous and revolting in that laugh, in those eyes, in such depravity in the face of a child. "What? At five years old?" Svidrigailov whispered in genuine horror. "What does this mean?" And now she turned to him, her little face all aglow, reaching out her arms... "Accursed child!" Svidrigailov cried, raising his hand to strike her — but at that moment he woke up.
He was in the same bed, still wrapped in the blanket. The candle had not been lit, and daylight was streaming through the windows.

"Nightmares all night!" He sat up, feeling utterly shattered; his bones ached. A thick fog hung outside, and he could see nothing. It was nearly five. He'd overslept! He got up and put on his still-damp jacket and overcoat. Feeling the revolver in his pocket, he took it out. Then he sat down, pulled a notebook from his pocket, and on the most prominent place on the title page wrote a few lines in large letters. He read them over, then sat thinking with his elbows on the table. The revolver and the notebook lay beside him. Some flies woke and settled on the untouched veal still sitting on the table. He stared at them, then began absently trying to catch one with his free right hand. He kept at it until he was tired, but couldn't catch it. Finally, realizing he was absorbed in this pointless pursuit, he came to himself with a start, got up, and walked resolutely out of the room. A minute later he was in the street.

A thick, milky fog lay over the city. Svidrigailov walked along the slippery, dirty wooden pavement toward the Little Neva. He was picturing the waters of the Little Neva, swollen in the night — Petrovsky Island, the wet paths, the wet grass, the wet trees and bushes — and finally, that bush... He began irritably staring at the buildings, trying to think of something else. Not a cab or a soul in the street. The bright yellow little wooden houses looked dirty and dejected with their shutters closed. The cold and damp penetrated his whole body, and he started shivering. Now and then he passed a shop sign and read each one carefully. At last he reached the end of the wooden pavement and came to a large stone building. A dirty, shivering dog crossed his path, tail between its legs. A man in a greatcoat lay face down across the sidewalk, dead drunk. He glanced at him and walked on. A tall tower loomed on his left. "Bah!" he exclaimed. "Here's a good enough place. Why bother with Petrovsky? At least there'll be an official witness."

He almost smiled at this new thought and turned into the street with the large building and the tower. At the great locked gates of the building stood a small man, his shoulder leaning against them, wrapped in a gray soldier's overcoat with a copper Achilles helmet on his head. He cast a drowsy, indifferent look at Svidrigailov. His face wore that perpetual expression of sour dejection so firmly stamped on every face of the Jewish race without exception. The two of them — Svidrigailov and Achilles — stared at each other for several minutes without speaking. Finally it struck Achilles as irregular that a sober man should be standing three steps away, staring at him and saying nothing.
"What do you want here?" he said, without moving or changing position.
"Nothing, brother. Good morning," Svidrigailov answered.
"This isn't the place."
"I'm going to foreign parts, brother."
"Foreign parts?"
"America."
"America."
Svidrigailov took out the revolver and cocked it. Achilles raised his eyebrows.
"I say — this is no place for jokes like that!"
"Why shouldn't it be the place?"
"Because it isn't."
"Well, brother, I don't mind that. It's a perfectly good spot. When they ask you, just say he was going to America."
He raised the revolver to his right temple.
"You can't do that here! This isn't the place!" cried Achilles, suddenly wide awake, his eyes growing bigger and bigger.
Svidrigailov pulled the trigger.
